items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books I - III
items.text:
*Below I am starting the book club, as promised previously. It has probably taken longer than I originally led on. I expect that this can be forgiven. Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

***

items.title: A Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club: Farber's Second Essay
items.text:
*Welcome to the third week of our book club reading* A Lodging for Wayfaring Men. *We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll be discussing Chapter 2 next Saturday, but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix A. They are short and accessible.*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

***

# Was there a time when all Bitcoiners wanted was to be able to withdraw from the existing system?

Farber opens with what sounds to my ears like a pretty classic description of the non-aggression principle (I will admit however, that I am a rather ignorant libertarian): all governments are based on violence. But then he has this somewhat startling line:

> If you have wondered why some of us are so determined to keep governments out of cyberspace, please understand that this is why. We've had enough of centralized force. We're removing the whole mechanism. We think it was a mistake from the beginning. We don't want there to be anything for the two percent to grab.

After reading it a second time, I spent a bit of time pondering whether we have succeeded in this endeavor of keeping governments out of cyberspace. The surface answer seems to be negative: governments control much of what happens in cyberspace -- and their powergrab seems to be quickly accelerating. But, perhaps their control is not so thorough as I imagine. ICANN and the IETF aren't government organizations (this is possibly easy to refute). I can have an encrypted chat with someone in a different country with relative ease (I think?) and there is Bitcoin.

Farber describes how cyberspace is not based on coercion:

> Things work by economic means here. If you don't like the way a market operates, just move to a different one. Or, if no one does it the way you think is right, start your own. There are no protected services here, and nothing mandatory. You may opt out of anything you don't like, or offer any service you like.
>
> The entire system is built around the idea that persuading people to trade with you is moral, and that forcing them is not.

Interestingly, he then makes the claim that such a system should be free of politics:

> Once you remove the mechanisms of coercion, you remove something else -- politics. Politics is the art and science of managing centralized coercion. This is the reason political debates are so infuriating: the final decision leads to unopposable force Once the political process is completed, you have the choice either to obey or to be punished.

And I think our experience of Bitcoin has been that its voluntary nature has definitely *not* removed politics -- although it may have made the results of politics far less damaging. At the end of the day, the people who seek to coerce have no choice but to walk away -- good riddance, BIP 110ers.

But that aside, Farber ultimately gets to this point:

> We do not want to control your governments. We are not asking to change your lives. We are only withdrawing from your game. Go your own way in peace.

Donning my rose-colored glasses for a minute, I like to think that there was some of this in the original Bitcoin ethos. Bitcoin is the exit, it's the way to opt-out from a system that we all perceive to be so twisted and coercive that it severely degrades the human experience. While I still hear most Bitcoiners parrot the message that fiat is bad, I think far fewer of us are content to withdraw from the system. We seem to want to take over the system.

Farber says:

> If we were simply one more reform movement, we would seek to conquer your system and run it our way.

This sounds much more like what Bitcoin culture has become. It's not enough that we peacefully withdraw and use bitcoin on our own, we want to destroy the fiat system.

So, I wonder: have we gone astray? Do you think Bitcoiner culture has come to hope for coercion more than self-sovereignty? If Bitcoin allows you to withdraw from the fiat game, is that enough for you -- even if the fiat game remains dominate mode of society (and the home of most of the number go up stuff)?

> One frequently told story is that these shifts are **in large part the result of corporate greed and capitalism.** The price of spending an evening in the kinds of places where people socialise — bars, pubs, restaurants, entertainment venues — has risen steeply, leading them to stay at home instead and therefore socialise less. Or the decline in reading is partly due to books becoming too expensive.

...but still, we do *this*:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161925)

## CONSEQUENTLY:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161926)

The SUMMARY is spot-on:

> Having friends over could be a 10/10 experience, but the house would need sorting out, and what if they have other plans? **Scrolling and streaming may only be a 6/10 by comparison but it’s a guaranteed 6: no risk, no effort.** It’s the same for reading. Getting lost in a great book is one of life’s great experiences and incredibly cheap at the price, but it demands effort.

> The question is whether knowing that the decline in socialising and reading is more about convenience than affordability is reassuring. If it were just about price, we have plenty of tools for dealing with that. Asking people to perpetually fight temptation and put long-term gains above short-term pleasure has a much weaker record

## Why are we so anti-social, stackers?

(...I ask, not my friends over dinner, but my internal pals over a screen. _makes sense, makes sense!_)

...and if you don't get the [Bowling Alone reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_Alone), it's from Robert Putnam's two-decades-old book on the decline of America's communities. 

***

items.text:
Beer is my go-to alcoholic beverage, but when I was childfree, the stars aligned such that I was able to partake in wine appreciation sessions for free. A French wine distributor, eager to build up its reputation, would organise free wine tasting sessions and educate the participants on the salient characteristics of its signature wines. Coupled with cheese and other finger foods, these sessions were as appetising as they were informative. Bonus points if the wine came in cute little bottles.

Not that I became able to discern the difference between good wine and bad wine, but I look back at these wine indulgences with fondness.

Is wine a regular fixture at your dinner events? If so, does red wine or white wine knock your socks off? Drinking wine in moderation has been known to aid memory retention, so maybe I should reduce my reliance on beer!

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

In the last year I have noticed that my mindset has turned more sour and i'm moving into this nihilistic/fatalistic worldview in which we as human beings as a whole are basically doomed. "The apes who invinted tools are fully in the process of f*cking it up" is basically the main thought atm. Now I know rationally that doomerism is not the way to go and I desperatly want to move back to a more balanced mindset, but let's say that it feels that I must forcefully (and cringefully) push myself into a positive thinking habit which feels like being unrealistic.

items.title: Bitkey Reflections: New and Old
items.text:
When I'm not shitposting, econ ranting, boomer bashing, or sharing mountain views, I *have* on occasion been writing about hardware wallets and other Bitcoin setup systems. https://stacker.news/items/800714

It's been a while.

## Introducing the bitkey, new and old:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161961)

***

I’ve used a bitkey as my main spend-and-receive hot wallet for the better part of two years. *(Level 2 in DarthCoin’s 1-2-3 rendition of bitcoin balances and how to secure them* https://stacker.news/items/302681)

So, when an odd tweet by the president of Próspera [proposed](https://x.com/JoelBomgar/status/2085752404146884772) to *send $250* in bitcoin for buying a new bitkey, I saw my cheap chance. *I am a shitposter with enough following; I want an upgraded bitkey with a screen; …and oh the \~20% arbitrage right off the top (since a bitkey plus delivery only cost me about $205) is juicy.* (Also: bitcoin's exchange rate today is some 25% higher than when Mr. Bomgar engaged in this little redistribution/marketing stunt, so I'll take the difference as my *just payout for the labor and inconvenience of setting it up*.) **Don't mind if I grab free shit**

The [guy spent some $25,000](https://x.com/JoelBomgar/status/2086553798042911105) to promote and supply a bunch of not-exactly-random strangers on the internet with a bitkey, *hoping* (in vain?) that they’d reciprocate *and* write about/video/share their experience with using what he says is “the most amazing bitcoin product ever.” Looking around, I can't say he got too much bang for his bucks (sats).

The *smart* play (and that presumably some of the \~100 unworthy recipients did) would have been to just take the dough and never talk to Mr. Bomgar again... then again, this is Bitcoin and those of us passionate about this space are pretty generous with our time, and reciprocal and honest in character.

## Kudos to Mr. Bomgar for doing this grassroots campaign on his own literal dime, and seems only fair that I give him the time of day to *actually* write up my unboxing/experience with using bitkey.

***

**The first edition, the screenless version I’ve used for a long time, is super convenient.** It’s a 2-of-3 multisig with keys distributed as *phone wallet app* + *physical rock-looking device* + *bitkey servers*, with the backup files (app key + emergency exit kit) stored and encrypted on my Google drive. (I have had no occasion to invoke these, and been too lazy to battle-test the features.)

Their big selling point was toward normies: *Abstract away from seed phrases and the pesky mechanics of Bitcoin* under-the-hood and just have a secure, functional wallet that any regular schmuck can use. (Even UTXOs are mostly hidden... you *can* display them and coin-control only via consolidating small ones... not the proper control and overview we're used to from HWWs.)

Recently, they’ve changed that tune and realized that part of their audience and clientele might also be *as a secondary/alternative* (or travel-friendly) setup for pretty dedicated Bitcoiners.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hiHjJtgaiVM

**I certainly fall in this category.** I *can*[^1] safeguard my own single-sig seedphrases and I *can* store my traditional hardware-in-cold-storage wallet appropriately. But I don’t touch those on a regular basis, and I certainly don’t want to (re)move them for travel purposes. Plus, taking stuff away from the house etc (presuming, indeed, that I keep the HWWs at home...), I’m always wary I’ll drop stuff or clumsily lose e.g., bags. The multisig/back-up feature gives nice peace of mind… plus, **the device looks like a decorative rook *anyways*,** and so offers some sort of privacy/opsec protection.

I certainly liked the gold-colored back and altogether *rock* feeling of the original bitkey. It was smooth and easy to use. TWO drawbacks with the original rock:

1. no screen/ability to [double-check](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2085814182721569071) fees, address, or amount of the tx that I’m signing.
2. inability to pick fee rates; even at low-fee options, even in our extreme low-fee environment, they seem too high – in the 200-500 sats range, *regardless* of the going blockspace price, weirdly higher now than \~a year ago. (In contrast, standard transactions from my other wallets easily reach into double-digit sats.) Fine, multisig is a heavier transaction type, but this is annoyingly on the nose.

The new one, while wider and with the benefits of a screen, feels more like... yet another screened device (https://stacker.news/items/1597013). It feels *slightly* more plastic-y and with the screen definitely more fragile.

The new bitkey comes in a flashy packaging, with the interior box having this nice, shiny tamperproof seal reading “Secured for life” on it. Unpacking it we get this Apple-like feel of quality product: slick, simple, no skimping on costs in even the irrelevant packaging department.

The contrast to the original version is:

* slightly lighter color
* somewhat thicker and larger
* the surface of the new one (with screen on the back) feels more plastic-y – but it could just be that the old one is used and greasy and has been lumped around everywhere.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161962)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161963)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161964)

***

## Migrating from old to new

In a recent interview with [Stephan Livera, Clay Garrett](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hiHjJtgaiVM) (bitkey lead at Block) described how replacing a physical device is as easy as a few clicks with the new hardware *and* waiting a mandatory 7-day security period… during which the company will literally spam you with emails and messages (in case, you know, there’s some malicious actor or noisy roommate or evil maid hack involved).

Like an idiot, I clicked *this* option instead of just setting up the new bitkey and moving the funds on-chain. (Turns out the transfer needed an on-chain TX *anyway* in the recovery process.)

Mimicking a recovery process, is what I was mostly excited (and terrified!) for. I'm glad I could/did this when it wasn't necessary and I could just wait it out, no biggie. Worse in e.g., a coldcard-type of situation. 

https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2108572045097218392

I waited a week, during which I received about \~3 notifications on the app, some on email, and another few on the associated (burner) phone. *Not that bad*, actually. 

The final recovery process itself was fairly smooth: a lot of clicks and taps between device and phone... and then it all worked.

Today I made the first tx. While I got precisely what I wanted (1), it *also* meant a few more extra taps and rounds of confirmation between device and phone. Before it was all just tap-tap-tap, *done*. Now: slightly clunkier.

***TL;DR:*** happy user, happy upgrade, great experience... and the best part, the additional sats became a beautiful carry trade... because obviously I didn't trust Mr. Bomgar, so I took his initial tx on a fresh on-chain wallet, paid bitkey with dirty fiat, and laundered the initial balance through Lightning. *Just in case* there was some spying/chainalysis spyware going on. (I probs fucked myself in some sense... but Luke says you can only protect yourself so much: https://stacker.news/items/1504762, https://stacker.news/items/1524157...)

***

Second, privileged/oh-no-woo-is-me observation: **What am I supposed to do with the old bitkey?**

items.title: Corisco: Open-source Lightning wallet where keys live on an HW device
items.text:
## Open-source Lightning wallet where keys live on an HW device and every payment is confirmed on the device (built on spark.money)

![](https://m.stacker.news/161968)

Welcome Corisco, a self-custodial Lightning wallet where private keys never touch your phone. They stay on a dedicated ESP32-S3 device, and every signature has to be confirmed on its own screen. It uses Spark's FROST-based signing, with Rust firmware and an Android app (soon IOS) over BLE.

It's early and not audited, so test with small amounts only. Everything is Apache-2.0, and you can try it in about 10 minutes with a LilyGo T-Display-S3.

Here is the repo https://github.com/corisco-wallet

--- 

> A self-custodial Lightning wallet where private keys live on a dedicated ESP32-S3 hardware device, not your phone. Every signature is confirmed physically on the device's own screen before it happens.
> 
> Built on [Spark](https://www.spark.money/)'s FROST-based threshold signing protocol.
> 
> ## Try it in 10 minutes
> 
> You need:
> 
> * A [LilyGo T-Display-S3](https://github.com/Xinyuan-LilyGO/T-Display-S3) and a USB data cable
> * An Android phone with Bluetooth (soon available for IOS)
> * A computer (Windows, macOS or Linux) with [Rust](https://rustup.rs/) installed, used only to flash
> 
> ### 1. Install the app
> 
> 1. On your phone, open the [latest app release](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/corisco-android-app/releases/latest).
> 2. Download `corisco-android-app-*.apk` and open it.
> 3. If Android asks, allow installs from your browser or file manager.
> 
> ### 2. Flash the firmware
> 
> 1. Download `esp32-lilygo-t-display-s3-firmware-*.bin` (the one **without** `-app`) from the [latest firmware release](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/corisco-firmware/releases/latest).
> 2. Install the flashing tool:
> 
>   ```
>   cargo install espflash
>   ```
> 3. Plug the T-Display-S3 into your computer and flash it:
> 
>   ```
>   espflash write-bin 0x0 esp32-lilygo-t-display-s3-firmware-*.bin
>   espflash reset
>   ```
> 
>   On Linux, if you get a permission error: `sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER`, then log out and back in.
> 
> ### 3. Set up the device
> 
> 1. The device boots to the Welcome screen: create a new wallet and set a PIN.
> 2. **Write down your recovery words** and keep them offline.
> 
> ### 4. Pair and use
> 
> 1. Open the Corisco app, turn Bluetooth on and pick your device (it shows up as `Corisco-<id>`).
> 2. Receive a payment, or send one and **confirm it on the device's screen**. Nothing is signed until you do.
> 
> Early software: test with small amounts only. Need a hand? [Open an issue](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/corisco-firmware/issues).
> 
> ## Repositories
> 
> * [**corisco-firmware**](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/corisco-firmware) -- the ESP32 hardware-signer firmware and the BLE wire protocol it defines.
> * [**corisco-android-app**](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/corisco-android-app) -- the React Native mobile app, tested against the firmware's protocol vectors.
> * [**crypto-core**](https://github.com/corisco-wallet/crypto-core) -- the platform-agnostic signing logic (BIP32/BIP39, FROST threshold signing, the leaf-ownership-transfer crypto) used by the firmware.
> 
> Start with `corisco-firmware`'s README for the architecture overview and a quickstart for each component.

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books I - III
items.text:
*Below I am starting the book club, as promised previously. It has probably taken longer than I originally led on. I expect that this can be forgiven. Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

***

items.title: A Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club: Farber's Second Essay
items.text:
*Welcome to the third week of our book club reading* A Lodging for Wayfaring Men. *We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll be discussing Chapter 2 next Saturday, but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix A. They are short and accessible.*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

***

# Was there a time when all Bitcoiners wanted was to be able to withdraw from the existing system?

Farber opens with what sounds to my ears like a pretty classic description of the non-aggression principle (I will admit however, that I am a rather ignorant libertarian): all governments are based on violence. But then he has this somewhat startling line:

> If you have wondered why some of us are so determined to keep governments out of cyberspace, please understand that this is why. We've had enough of centralized force. We're removing the whole mechanism. We think it was a mistake from the beginning. We don't want there to be anything for the two percent to grab.

After reading it a second time, I spent a bit of time pondering whether we have succeeded in this endeavor of keeping governments out of cyberspace. The surface answer seems to be negative: governments control much of what happens in cyberspace -- and their powergrab seems to be quickly accelerating. But, perhaps their control is not so thorough as I imagine. ICANN and the IETF aren't government organizations (this is possibly easy to refute). I can have an encrypted chat with someone in a different country with relative ease (I think?) and there is Bitcoin.

Farber describes how cyberspace is not based on coercion:

> Things work by economic means here. If you don't like the way a market operates, just move to a different one. Or, if no one does it the way you think is right, start your own. There are no protected services here, and nothing mandatory. You may opt out of anything you don't like, or offer any service you like.
>
> The entire system is built around the idea that persuading people to trade with you is moral, and that forcing them is not.

Interestingly, he then makes the claim that such a system should be free of politics:

> Once you remove the mechanisms of coercion, you remove something else -- politics. Politics is the art and science of managing centralized coercion. This is the reason political debates are so infuriating: the final decision leads to unopposable force Once the political process is completed, you have the choice either to obey or to be punished.

And I think our experience of Bitcoin has been that its voluntary nature has definitely *not* removed politics -- although it may have made the results of politics far less damaging. At the end of the day, the people who seek to coerce have no choice but to walk away -- good riddance, BIP 110ers.

But that aside, Farber ultimately gets to this point:

> We do not want to control your governments. We are not asking to change your lives. We are only withdrawing from your game. Go your own way in peace.

Donning my rose-colored glasses for a minute, I like to think that there was some of this in the original Bitcoin ethos. Bitcoin is the exit, it's the way to opt-out from a system that we all perceive to be so twisted and coercive that it severely degrades the human experience. While I still hear most Bitcoiners parrot the message that fiat is bad, I think far fewer of us are content to withdraw from the system. We seem to want to take over the system.

Farber says:

> If we were simply one more reform movement, we would seek to conquer your system and run it our way.

This sounds much more like what Bitcoin culture has become. It's not enough that we peacefully withdraw and use bitcoin on our own, we want to destroy the fiat system.

So, I wonder: have we gone astray? Do you think Bitcoiner culture has come to hope for coercion more than self-sovereignty? If Bitcoin allows you to withdraw from the fiat game, is that enough for you -- even if the fiat game remains dominate mode of society (and the home of most of the number go up stuff)?

items.title: Screens Taking Over: Why Are We "Bowling Alone"? (FT, John Burn-Murdoch)
items.text:
Crazy good piece by our friend Mr Murdoch: (real) prices of going out has increased quite a bit both in the UK and US... but we're not transferring socializing to cheaper/at-home events. We just basically stop hanging out with others. 

![](https://m.stacker.news/161924)

> One frequently told story is that these shifts are **in large part the result of corporate greed and capitalism.** The price of spending an evening in the kinds of places where people socialise — bars, pubs, restaurants, entertainment venues — has risen steeply, leading them to stay at home instead and therefore socialise less. Or the decline in reading is partly due to books becoming too expensive.

...but still, we do *this*:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161925)

## CONSEQUENTLY:

![](https://m.stacker.news/161926)

The SUMMARY is spot-on:

> Having friends over could be a 10/10 experience, but the house would need sorting out, and what if they have other plans? **Scrolling and streaming may only be a 6/10 by comparison but it’s a guaranteed 6: no risk, no effort.** It’s the same for reading. Getting lost in a great book is one of life’s great experiences and incredibly cheap at the price, but it demands effort.

> The question is whether knowing that the decline in socialising and reading is more about convenience than affordability is reassuring. If it were just about price, we have plenty of tools for dealing with that. Asking people to perpetually fight temptation and put long-term gains above short-term pleasure has a much weaker record

## Why are we so anti-social, stackers?

(...I ask, not my friends over dinner, but my internal pals over a screen. _makes sense, makes sense!_)

...and if you don't get the [Bowling Alone reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_Alone), it's from Robert Putnam's two-decades-old book on the decline of America's communities. 

***

items.title: My wine drinking days
items.text:
Beer is my go-to alcoholic beverage, but when I was childfree, the stars aligned such that I was able to partake in wine appreciation sessions for free. A French wine distributor, eager to build up its reputation, would organise free wine tasting sessions and educate the participants on the salient characteristics of its signature wines. Coupled with cheese and other finger foods, these sessions were as appetising as they were informative. Bonus points if the wine came in cute little bottles.

Not that I became able to discern the difference between good wine and bad wine, but I look back at these wine indulgences with fondness.

Is wine a regular fixture at your dinner events? If so, does red wine or white wine knock your socks off? Drinking wine in moderation has been known to aid memory retention, so maybe I should reduce my reliance on beer!

https://www.d.umn.edu/cla/faculty/troufs/anthfood/images/OurDailyBread_cows.jpg
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y3_1IdrPreE

"Welcome to the world of industrial food production and high-tech farming! To the rhythm of conveyor belts and immense machines, the film looks without commenting into the places where food is produced in Europe: monumental spaces, surreal landscapes and bizarre sounds - a cool, industrial environment which leaves little space for individualism. People, animals, crops and machines play a supporting role in the logistic of this system which provides our society's standard of living. OUR DAILY BREAD is a wide-screen tableau of a feast which isn't always easy to digest - and in which we all take part. A pure, meticulous and high-end film experience that enables the audience to form their own ideas."
